prompt: Build the booking page for Willowmere Veterinary, a small neighborhood animal clinic. It needs a header with the clinic name and phone (555-0142), a short welcome line, a three-step 'book a visit' area (pick a service, pick a day, confirm), a list of three services (Wellness exam, Vaccinations, Dental cleaning) with prices, and an emergency notice for after-hours care. Owners have said the current site feels cold and clinical; the clinic wants it to feel calm and trustworthy. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: The page has one clearly dominant brand color used for the main action and key accents, not several competing hues.
Page background, cards and body text form a coherent set of neutrals, and the neutrals are not pure black on pure white nor an unrelated gray.
Body text, prices and button labels are comfortably readable against the backgrounds they sit on, including any tinted card or notice.
The emergency notice is distinguishable from ordinary content through color without looking alarming or clashing with the rest of the page.
The overall impression is calm and warm rather than clinical or candy-colored.
Identifies concrete problems in the palette itself (for example too many unrelated hues competing, or status colors that also read as brand or action colors) rather than generic taste comments.
Flags at least one real legibility problem by naming the specific pair, such as white text on the yellow delayed color or light gray meta text on white or the light page.
Proposes specific replacement values or clear adjustments, not just 'make it better'.
Keeps what already works, such as the neutral page and panel scheme or the blue primary action, rather than discarding everything.
Is organized so a developer could act on it in order of importance.

prompt: We are naming the color for Kestrel Code Club, an after-school coding program for ages 8 to 12, run by a nonprofit. The logo is a simple bird silhouette. We have narrowed the lead color to three options: #ff5a36 (a bright orange-red), #2a9d8f (a mid teal), or #3a2e8c (a deep indigo). It will appear on the website, on printed flyers handed out at schools, and on small embroidered patches. Which should we pick, and what should sit alongside it? Please keep it practical.
rubric: Commits to one of the three options and explains the choice with reference to the audience and the stated uses (web, flyers, patches).
Considers how the chosen color behaves as a background and as text or a button, not only how it looks as a swatch.
Suggests supporting colors (neutrals and at most one or two accents) with specific values rather than a vague description.
Notes at least one practical limitation or adjustment for the chosen color, such as needing a darker shade for text or a lighter tint for backgrounds.
Does not pad the answer with a long theory of color or list every option exhaustively.

prompt: Make a dark-mode screen for Tidepool, a companion app for a tabletop role-playing game. Show a character sheet card: name 'Marrow Vance, Tide Warden', level 7, health 34/48 as a bar, three stat chips (Strength 14, Wits 17, Nerve 11), an inventory list with four items (Salt-iron blade, Lantern, Net of pearls, Healing draught), and a row with buttons 'Roll', 'Rest' and 'Level up'. The players use it in dim rooms at night. Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: The surface colors have visible, controlled steps (page, card, raised element) so layers read as layers instead of one flat black block.
The page is not pure black with pure white text; text and surfaces are softened enough that the screen is not glaring in a dim room.
The health bar, stat chips and buttons are each easy to tell apart and the primary button is clearly the most prominent.
Accent and status colors (health, level up) look deliberate on the dark surfaces and are not neon, vibrating or muddy.
All text, including secondary text on cards, remains comfortably readable.
Recognizes that the existing palette is already coherent and legible and says so plainly instead of inventing problems.
Recommends no changes or only a small number of minor, clearly justified ones, and does not propose a new palette or a redesign.
Any suggested change is specific (names the selector and a value) and explains the practical benefit.
Does not swap the established green and cream identity for different hues.

prompt: On our scheduling tool, Plumbline, the red error text (#d92d20) looks sharp on the white form, but on the tan notice banner (#e9dcc3) where we show the same error it looks muddy and harder to read, and the green success text (#12b76a) on the same banner almost disappears. Why does that happen, and what should we do so the messages work in both places?
rubric: Explains that the same color reads differently depending on the background it sits on, and connects this to the tan banner's lightness and warmth.
Gives a believable reason the green success text fails specifically, such as too little lightness difference from the light tan banner.
Offers specific fixes, such as darker text shades for use on the banner, or changing the banner background, with concrete values.
Mentions that status meaning should not depend on color alone, or suggests an icon or label, or otherwise keeps messages understandable without relying on hue.
Is concise and answers the question asked without a lecture on general color theory.

prompt: We are redesigning the donation page for Harbor Light, a nonprofit that runs a winter shelter. The page sections, top to bottom: a top bar with logo and 'Give' button, a hero with a photo of the shelter and the headline 'Keep the lights on through winter', a row of three suggested amounts ($25, $60, $120) with a 'Donate now' button, a section of three short impact stories, a progress bar showing $41,200 raised of $60,000, and a dark footer with contact details and a tax-deductibility note. Describe how you would assign colors across these sections so the page feels warm and trustworthy and the donate action is unmistakable. Give actual hex values and say where each is used.
rubric: Assigns a specific hex value to each major element or section rather than only describing moods.
Makes the donate action the single most prominent colored element and keeps other buttons and accents visibly quieter.
Uses a small, coherent set of colors (one lead color, a neutral family, at most one or two accents) rather than a different color per section.
Addresses text over the hero photo and on the dark footer, with a way to keep it readable.
The progress bar and impact stories are colored in a way that supports the page instead of competing with the donate action.

prompt: Build a one-screen landing page for Brightwater Pools, a pool-service company. Their brand guidelines say the brand color is #ff6a00 (a strong orange) and it must be used as given for the logo block and the main button. The page needs: a header with the logo block and phone number, a headline, a two-sentence description, a 'Get a free quote' button, and three small cards (Weekly cleaning, Chemical balancing, Equipment repair). Deliver a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, and no external assets.
rubric: The exact #ff6a00 is used for the logo block and the main button; it is not replaced by a different orange.
Text placed on the orange has enough contrast to read, handled by choosing the text color carefully rather than by changing the brand color.
The rest of the page (backgrounds, cards, secondary text) uses restrained neutrals or a muted supporting color, so the orange stays the focal point and is not repeated everywhere.
The large orange areas are limited so the page does not feel loud or tiring.
The page looks cohesive and professional rather than a stack of unrelated colors.

prompt: Quick one. We have light gray placeholder text (#9a9a9a) inside the white search box on our recipe app, Panfry. Is that okay, or should it change? Two or three sentences at most, please.
rubric: Gives a clear verdict (it is too light or borderline and should be darkened) instead of hedging.
Offers a specific replacement value or a direction such as a darker gray.
Keeps to roughly three sentences or fewer, with no headings, lists or lectures.
Does not contradict itself or add unrelated recommendations.
The result uses one lead color and a small set of related neutrals instead of many saturated unrelated hues.
All text, including button labels, is clearly readable against its background.
Cards, header and welcome area feel like one family and the primary actions are distinguishable from the surroundings.
The overall impression is trustworthy and sober, appropriate for a bookkeeping firm.
The content and structure are preserved (same header, welcome, two cards with buttons, and note) with no invented features.
